apps.name: PaintBoard

headline: Open it and
draw
landing.lede: No account. No tutorial. No subscription. A sketchpad that is ready the moment the screen is, and gets out of the way after that.
left_out: A cloud that holds your drawings
what_remains: Eighteen colours, chosen once so you don't have to
Four tools: brush, pencil, marker, eraser
Text you can drag, resize and rotate
Any photo as the canvas background
Full offline use — the network is only for ads
Export or share as PNG, straight from the canvas
features: Brush, pencil, marker and eraser — each with its own weight and edge, not one slider pretending to be four.
A fixed palette. No wheel, no hex field, no decision to make before the first stroke.
Type anywhere, then move, resize or rotate it. It lives in the drawing, so the eraser treats it like ink.
Drop in a photo and draw over it. The photo never leaves the device.
Pinch to zoom for detail, rotate the canvas ninety degrees when the drawing wants a different orientation.
One tap to save to your photos or hand it to any other app.
landing._paletteNote: The real kPaletteColors from lib/models/drawing_models.dart in the drawing repo. Update here if that list ever changes.
shots: A hand-drawn sketch of hills, grass and a sun on PaintBoard's white canvas, with the tool panel and colour palette on the right
The whole app. One screen, no menus.
Korean text typed onto the same sketch, over a lilac background
Text behaves like ink — it can be drawn over, and erased.
The same sketch with the canvas background filled sky blue from the palette
One tap fills the background — the drawing stays on top.

paragraphs: I wrote the first version in 2017 as a native iOS app, for one reason: I wanted to sketch something quickly and every app on my phone made me set up first.

This year I rewrote it from nothing in Flutter, so the Android half of the world could have it too. The rewrite was almost entirely an exercise in restraint — the temptation to add layers, brushes and a colour wheel is constant, and every one of them would have cost the thing that makes it useful.
It is still one screen. It still opens in under a second. It still has eighteen colours.
timeline: First release — native Swift, iPhone and iPad

landing.sibling: There's also PaintBoardPro on the App Store — a separate app with a full colour picker, not a paid tier of this one. PaintBoard is deliberately the simpler of the two, and it stays free.
